newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac takes another gamble.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac takes another gamble.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac's decision to call a snap parliamentary election bears all the hallmarks of a man who loves a gamble and has no qualms about changing his mind.
His expected announcement of an election nine months early flatly belies a statement last July that dissolving parliament would only be justified if France hit a political crisis.
Rather than let his Gaullist party in parliament sail on with a huge majority towards an uncertain vote due next March, he has chosen to try catch the left-wing opposition unprepared.
But it is a high-stakes gamble, because Prime Minister Alain Juppe's public approval rating, and Chirac's own standing in the polls, have for months been at near-record lows.
A defeat for the Gaullists could make Chirac a lame duck president for much of the rest of a seven-year term that ends in 2002.
The challenge fits the forceful 64-year-old head of state who, like his political mentor General Charles de Gaulle, has always preferred to command rather than follow the course of events.
Gambles and turnabouts have marked Chirac's 30-year career as well as his first two years in power since May 1995.
One of his first decisions was to order a resumption of French nuclear tests in the South Pacific, triggering a furore just as the world was discussing a global testing ban.

Chirac weathered the storm and his gamble paid off. Protests abated when, convinced he had made France's nuclear strike force operational into the 21st century, he announced that tests were over for ever.
Breaking with De Gaulle's fierce nationalism, Chirac then began moves to bring France back into the military wing of NATO.
On the domestic scene, he quickly abandoned campaign pledges to make the fight against record unemployment and what he called France's "social fracture" his top priority.
"Election promises only commit those who listen to them," he once quipped in a throwaway line that has stuck to him.
Once a lukewarm supporter of European monetary union, Chirac made joining the European single currency his top goal.
Within six months, priorities shifted to curbing public spending and reforming the welfare system to cut deficits and comply with the Maastricht Treaty's requirements.
His popularity plunged. A public transport strike paralysed the country for weeks. But he remained unperturbed, rejecting strong pressure to fire Juppe.
Twice prime minister, twice beaten in previous presidential bids, Chirac has taken many punches and suffered periods in the political wilderness.

More than once, opponents have declared his career finished, not least when he battled the seemingly unbeatable lead of his fellow-Gaullist rival, then prime minister Edouard Balladur, in the campaign for the May 1995 election.
Winning the presidency at his third bid was another of the feats of will power that earned him the nickname "Bulldozer".
Chirac prides himself on being a pragmatist. Friends say he is a kind, sensitive man who commands fierce loyalty.
Foes see him as an opportunist with no fixed views who tends to act before thinking.
Born on November 29, 1932, the son of a businessman with roots in rural Correze in central France, Chirac graduated from the elite civil service school Ecole Nationale d'Administration.
He entered government at the tender age of 34, making a strong mark as farm minister, and became prime minister at 41.
He has maintained those rural roots, regularly consulting his friends in Correze as a grassroots political barometer.

After resigning as prime minister in a power struggle with President Valery Giscard d'Estaing in 1976, he was elected mayor of Paris in 1977, building a power base for his first presidential bid in 1981 which split the right and helped assure victory for the late Socialist Francois Mitterrand.
When the centre-right won 1986 parliamentary elections, Chirac became prime minister in an unprecedented power sharing arrangement with Mitterrand, dubbed "cohabitation".
He lost to Mitterrand in his second bid for the presidency two years later but clawed his way back after crushing attempts to oust him from the leadership of the Gaullist RPR party.
